claim: Climate change is characterized by increased temperatures and altered precipitation patterns.

claim: Drought adversely affects tree productivity.
source: Drought adversely affects forest health in many aspects, including seedling recruitment (Pozner et al., 2022), tree productivity (Klein et al., 2014), and mortality of trees (Klein et al., 2019), with increased susceptibility to pathogen or insect attack (Reichstein et al., 2013; McDowell et al., 2022).

claim: Drought adversely affects mortality of trees.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016.

claim: Root systems provide physical stabilization.
source: Root systems mediate water and nutrient uptake, provide physical stabilization, store nutrients and carbohydrates, and provide carbon and nutrients to the soil through the process of fine-root turnover (Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016.

claim: Root systems store nutrients and carbohydrates.
source: Root systems mediate water and nutrient uptake, provide physical stabilization, store nutrients and carbohydrates, and provide carbon and nutrients to the soil through the process of fine-root turnover (Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016.

claim: Root systems provide carbon and nutrients to the soil through the process of fine-root turnover.
source: Root systems mediate water and nutrient uptake, provide physical stabilization, store nutrients and carbohydrates, and provide carbon and nutrients to the soil through the process of fine-root turnover (Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brunner and Godbold, 2007; Haichar et al., 2008; Ryan, 2011; Harfouche et al., 2014; Jarzyniak and Jasiński, 2014; Klein et al., 2016.

claim: Trees invest a substantial part of their photosynthesized carbon into root exudates that entice and presumably feed plant-beneficial and root-associated microbiota.
source: In addition to these roles, trees invest a substantial part of their photosynthesized carbon into root exudates that entice and presumably feed plant-beneficial and root-associated microbiota (Bais et al., 2006; Badri and Vivanco, 2009; Karst et al., 2017; Jakoby et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bais et al., 2006; Badri and Vivanco, 2009; Karst et al., 2017; Jakoby et al., 2020.

claim: Rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth through various mechanisms such as increasing the availability of nutrients.
source: In parallel, the rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth through various mechanisms such as increasing the availability of nutrients, secreting phytohormones, suppressing pathogens, or having positive effects on the plant metabolism (Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth by secreting phytohormones.
source: In parallel, the rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth through various mechanisms such as increasing the availability of nutrients, secreting phytohormones, suppressing pathogens, or having positive effects on the plant metabolism (Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth by suppressing pathogens.
source: In parallel, the rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth through various mechanisms such as increasing the availability of nutrients, secreting phytohormones, suppressing pathogens, or having positive effects on the plant metabolism (Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth by having positive effects on the plant metabolism.
source: In parallel, the rhizosphere microbes can promote plant growth through various mechanisms such as increasing the availability of nutrients, secreting phytohormones, suppressing pathogens, or having positive effects on the plant metabolism (Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pérez-Montaño et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Microbial utilization and metabolism play a central role in modulating concentration gradients of a variety of compounds right outside root tips, thereby constituting a soil sink.
source: Microbial utilization and metabolism play a central role in modulating concentration gradients of a variety of compounds right outside root tips, thereby constituting a soil sink (Dakora and Phillips, 2002; Mommer et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2017; Tsunoda and van Dam, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dakora and Phillips, 2002; Mommer et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2017; Tsunoda and van Dam, 2017.

claim: The majority of root exudates typically consists of 20% primary metabolites (sugars, amino acids, and organic acids).
source: The majority of root exudates typically consists of primary metabolites (20%; sugars, amino acids, and organic acids) and 15% of nitrogen as well as secondary metabolites, complex polymers, such as flavonoids, glucosinolates, auxins, etc. (Vives-Peris et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vives-Peris et al., 2020.

claim: Root exudates typically consist of 15% nitrogen.
source: The majority of root exudates typically consists of primary metabolites (20%; sugars, amino acids, and organic acids) and 15% of nitrogen as well as secondary metabolites, complex polymers, such as flavonoids, glucosinolates, auxins, etc. (Vives-Peris et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vives-Peris et al., 2020.

claim: Root exudates include secondary metabolites, complex polymers, such as flavonoids, glucosinolates, auxins.
source: The majority of root exudates typically consists of primary metabolites (20%; sugars, amino acids, and organic acids) and 15% of nitrogen as well as secondary metabolites, complex polymers, such as flavonoids, glucosinolates, auxins, etc. (Vives-Peris et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vives-Peris et al., 2020.

claim: Plant-derived metabolites shape microbial communities by allowing bacteria to metabolize them and then establish themselves in the rhizosphere.
source: Those plant-derived metabolites were shown to shape microbial communities by allowing bacteria to metabolize them and then establish themselves in the rhizosphere (Venturi and Keel, 2016; Sasse et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Venturi and Keel, 2016; Sasse et al., 2017.

claim: Root exudation is ubiquitous among tree species.
source: Although root exudation is ubiquitous among tree species, the amount and composition of root exudates vary.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about root exudation.

claim: The amount and composition of root exudates vary among tree species.
source: Although root exudation is ubiquitous among tree species, the amount and composition of root exudates vary.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about root exudation.

claim: Little information is available on how drought influences tree root exudates, their chemical composition, and how root metabolism is connected with shifts in root-associated microbiome composition.
source: So far, little information is available on how drought influences tree root exudates, their chemical composition, and how root metabolism is connected with shifts in root-associated microbiome composition (Tückmantel et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tückmantel et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2018.

claim: Oak trees (Quercus ilex) shift their exudates from primary to secondary metabolites under drought.
source: Recently, it was shown that oak trees (Quercus ilex) shift their exudates from primary to secondary metabolites under drought (Gargallo-Garriga et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gargallo-Garriga et al., 2018.

claim: The chemical composition of root exudates have a direct effect on the rhizosphere communities.
source: The chemical composition of root exudates have a direct effect on the rhizosphere communities.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about root exudates and rhizosphere communities.

claim: Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) genera include Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter, Burkholderia, Arthrobacter, and Paenibacillus.
source: These include plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) genera such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, Acinetobacter, Burkholderia, Arthrobacter, and Paenibacillus (Sasse et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sasse et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: The banana root exudate fumaric acid attracts the Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis N11 and stimulates biofilm formation.
source: For example, the banana root exudate fumaric acid attracts the Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis N11 and stimulates biofilm formation (Zhang et al., 2014); malic acid exuded by Arabidopsis stimulates binding to roots and biofilm formation on roots by the B. subtilis strain FB17 (Rudrappa et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Malic acid exuded by Arabidopsis stimulates binding to roots and biofilm formation on roots by the B. subtilis strain FB17.
source: For example, the banana root exudate fumaric acid attracts the Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis N11 and stimulates biofilm formation (Zhang et al., 2014); malic acid exuded by Arabidopsis stimulates binding to roots and biofilm formation on roots by the B. subtilis strain FB17 (Rudrappa et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rudrappa et al., 2008.

claim: Bacterial growth and antifungal activity of certain species of the Gram-negative Pseudomonas spp. is dependent on organic acids and sugars isolated from tomato root exudates.
source: Bacterial growth and antifungal activity of certain species of the Gram-negative Pseudomonas spp. is dependent on organic acids and sugars isolated from tomato root exudates (Kravchenko et al., 2003; Mhlongo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kravchenko et al., 2003; Mhlongo et al., 2018.

claim: Species of Pseudomonas and Bacillus are the best studied as models for beneficial plant-microbe interaction.
source: Among PGPR, species of Pseudomonas and Bacillus are the best studied as models for beneficial plant-microbe interaction (Weller et al., 2002; Raaijmakers et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weller et al., 2002; Raaijmakers et al., 2010.

claim: The importance of Pseudomonas and Bacillus genera to plants has been verified in multiple metagenomic studies.
source: Interestingly, the importance of both genera to plants has been verified in multiple metagenomic studies (Loper et al., 2012; Mendes et al., 2013), however, the interplay between these important root bacteria and forest trees remains a mystery.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Loper et al., 2012; Mendes et al., 2013.

claim: The interplay between Pseudomonas and Bacillus and forest trees remains a mystery.
source: Interestingly, the importance of both genera to plants has been verified in multiple metagenomic studies (Loper et al., 2012; Mendes et al., 2013), however, the interplay between these important root bacteria and forest trees remains a mystery.
evidence: The claim is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: In the forest soil, root exudation is suspected to enhance rhizobacteria, in turn leading to increased decomposition of soil organic matter, that is, increased C mineralization, a process termed microbial priming.
source: In the forest soil, root exudation is suspected to enhance rhizobacteria, in turn leading to increased decomposition of soil organic matter, that is, increased C mineralization, a process termed microbial priming (Schleppi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schleppi et al., 2019.

claim: Roots of both conifer and broadleaf tree species in an evergreen Mediterranean forest increase their exudation flux during the long dry season.
source: Recently, we have shown that roots of both conifer and broadleaf tree species in an evergreen Mediterranean forest increase their exudation flux during the long dry season (Jakoby et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jakoby et al., 2020, which is a prior study by the authors.

claim: The increase in exudation during the dry season occurred in spite of the sharp decrease in photosynthesis throughout the dry season.
source: This increase in exudation occurred in spite of the sharp decrease in photosynthesis throughout the dry season, and more so in the coniferous Cupressus sempervirens.
evidence: The claim is based on prior observations by the authors.

claim: Soil moisture declined gradually in drought trees down to <10% (V/V) 3 weeks following irrigation cessation.
source: Soil moisture declined gradually in drought trees down to <10% (V/V) 3 weeks following irrigation cessation, and increased back after re-irrigation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Assimilation and stomatal conductance of watered trees fluctuated around 8–12 µmol CO2 m–2 s–1 and 150–300 mol H2O m–2 s–1 throughout the experiment, respectively.
source: Assimilation and stomatal conductance of watered trees fluctuated around 8–12 µmol CO2 m–2 s–1 and 150–300 mol H2O m–2 s–1 throughout the experiment, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In drought trees, assimilation and stomatal conductance decreased to zero within 4 weeks.
source: In drought trees, these high rates decreased to zero within 4 weeks, and, upon re-irrigation, increased back to baseline values within 4–5 weeks.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of gas exchange measurements.

claim: Upon re-irrigation, assimilation and stomatal conductance increased back to baseline values within 4–5 weeks.
source: In drought trees, these high rates decreased to zero within 4 weeks, and, upon re-irrigation, increased back to baseline values within 4–5 weeks.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of gas exchange measurements.

claim: Bacterial inoculations had no effect on leaf gas exchange.
source: Bacterial inoculations had no effect on leaf gas exchange, and hence the interaction irrigation:bacteria was not significant either.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of gas exchange data.

claim: During the experiment, sapling biomass increment was 188.6±15.6 and 149.1±14.4 g for irrigated saplings with and without bacterial inoculations, respectively.
source: During the experiment, sapling biomass increment was 188.6±15.6 and 149.1±14.4 g for irrigated saplings with and without bacterial inoculations, respectively (difference not significant; p=0.753; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on biomass measurements.

claim: The effect of drought on biomass increment was highly significant (p<0.001).
source: The effect of drought was highly significant (p<0.001), and biomass increment in drought-exposed saplings with and without bacterial inoculations was 22.4±5.7 and 4.5±4.6 g, respectively (p=0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of biomass data.

claim: Biomass increment in drought-exposed saplings with and without bacterial inoculations was 22.4±5.7 and 4.5±4.6 g, respectively.
source: The effect of drought was highly significant (p<0.001), and biomass increment in drought-exposed saplings with and without bacterial inoculations was 22.4±5.7 and 4.5±4.6 g, respectively (p=0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on biomass measurements.

claim: Fluorescently tagged B. subtilis and P. stutzeri showed attachment and dispersed colonization along Cupressus fine roots, regardless of irrigation, on days 1 and 3 following inoculation.
source: Fluorescently tagged B. subtilis and P. stutzeri, that were modified from native strains isolated from the forest soil, showed attachment and dispersed colonization along Cupressus fine roots, regardless of irrigation, on days 1 and 3 following inoculation (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bacteria seemed to localize along crevices in the root epidermis, forming lines along roots, and sometimes co-localized.
source: Bacteria seemed to localize along crevices in the root epidermis, forming lines along roots, and sometimes co-localized (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Upon inoculation, P. stutzeri had higher abundance (~90%) than B. subtilis.
source: Upon inoculation, P. stutzeri had higher abundance (~90%) than B. subtilis, but this ratio reversed within a few days or weeks (Figure 1B), with B. subtilis having an advantage over P. stutzeri in drought trees.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ratio of P. stutzeri to B. subtilis reversed within a few days or weeks, with B. subtilis having an advantage over P. stutzeri in drought trees.
source: Upon inoculation, P. stutzeri had higher abundance (~90%) than B. subtilis, but this ratio reversed within a few days or weeks (Figure 1B), with B. subtilis having an advantage over P. stutzeri in drought trees.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When irrigation was restored, the drought trees recruited the bacteria in a similar fashion to irrigated trees, with P. stutzeri exhibiting 80% abundance in the rhizosphere at day 3, and then substituted by B. subtilis at days 7 and 15.
source: Interestingly, when irrigation was restored, the drought trees recruited the bacteria in a similar fashion to irrigated trees, with P. stutzeri exhibiting 80% abundance in the rhizosphere at day 3, and then substituted by B. subtilis at days 7 and 15 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Differences between days in relative abundance were significant (p<0.001), except for the difference between days 3 and 15 in soil under drought.
source: Differences between days in relative abundance were significant (p<0.001; Figure 1—source data 1), except for the difference between days 3 and 15 in soil under drought.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of bacterial abundance data.

claim: Bacterial abundance decreased over time, but was always ~10-fold higher in the rhizosphere than in the bulk soil.
source: Bacterial abundance decreased over time, but, importantly, was always ~10-fold higher in the rhizosphere than in the bulk soil (Figure 1B), further evidencing recruitment by roots.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bacterial abundance was lower in drought trees than around irrigated or re-irrigated trees (p<0.001).
source: Bacterial abundance was also lower in drought trees than around irrigated (Figure 1B) or re-irrigated trees (Figure 1C) (p<0.001; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of bacterial count data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Only in trees under constant irrigation and after two inoculations, bacterial communities of B. subtilis and P. stutzeri seemed to stabilize in the rhizosphere.
source: Overall, only in trees under constant irrigation and after two inoculations, bacterial communities of B. subtilis and P. stutzeri seemed to stabilize in the rhizosphere (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on observations of bacterial dynamics shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Under constant irrigation and under drought, bacterial inoculation significantly increased root exudation, by two- to threefold (p<0.001).
source: Under constant irrigation and under drought, bacterial inoculation significantly increased root exudation, by two- to threefold (Figure 2; p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of exudation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In trees that were exposed to drought and then re-irrigated, bacterial inoculation resulted in slightly lower exudates than without bacteria.
source: However, in trees that were exposed to drought and then re-irrigated, this pattern reversed, and inoculated trees had slightly lower exudates than without bacteria.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of exudation rates.

claim: Drought-exposed trees that were responsive to inoculation showed an ~50% increase in root exudation.
source: Thus, drought-exposed trees, that were responsive to inoculation, showing an ~50% increase in root exudation, lost this response when re-irrigated (p=0.039 for the interaction irrigation:bacteria).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of exudation data.

claim: The amount of organic carbon exuded from roots of drought-exposed trees was significantly, ~50% lower than from roots of irrigated trees.
source: The amount of organic carbon exuded from roots of drought-exposed trees was significantly, ~50% lower than from roots of irrigated trees, and moreover, ~70% lower, in the re-irrigation period (across inoculation treatments; p<0.01; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of exudation data.

claim: The amount of organic carbon exuded from roots of drought-exposed trees was ~70% lower in the re-irrigation period compared to irrigated trees.
source: The amount of organic carbon exuded from roots of drought-exposed trees was significantly, ~50% lower than from roots of irrigated trees, and moreover, ~70% lower, in the re-irrigation period (across inoculation treatments; p<0.01; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of exudation data.

claim: The same trees that were exposed to drought reduced their exudation when re-irrigated.
source: Importantly, the same trees that were exposed to drought reduced their exudation when re-irrigated (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by exudation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Correlation coefficients between root exudation rates and the abundance of B. subtilis and P. stutzeri in the rhizosphere yielded values above 0.5 for drought trees on day 3 following inoculation (p=0.046 for P. stutzeri).
source: This observation is further supported by examining correlation coefficients between root exudation rates and the abundance of B. subtilis and P. stutzeri in the rhizosphere. They yielded values above 0.5 for drought trees on day 3 following inoculation (Figure 2C; p=0.046 for P. stutzeri).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For B. subtilis, there was a high correlation with irrigated trees' exudation on day 7 following inoculation (p=0.093).
source: For B. subtilis, there was a high correlation also with irrigated trees' exudation on day 7 following inoculation (p=0.093).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Correlation coefficients between root exudation rates and bacterial abundance decreased in the re-irrigation period.
source: Correlation coefficients decreased in the re-irrigation period, and were negative in trees that were constantly irrigated.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of exudation and bacterial abundance data.

claim: The ratio between exudation rate and net assimilation rate was 0.40–0.45 under drought.
source: An additional measure of tree carbon allocation into root exudation is the ratio between exudation rate (µg C mg root–1 day–1) and net assimilation rate (µmol C m–2 leaf s–1). This ratio was 0.40–0.45 under drought, decreasing to 0.27–0.35 under re-irrigation (across inoculation treatments).
evidence: The claim is based on calculated ratios from experimental data.

claim: The ratio between exudation rate and net assimilation rate decreased to 0.27–0.35 under re-irrigation.
source: An additional measure of tree carbon allocation into root exudation is the ratio between exudation rate (µg C mg root–1 day–1) and net assimilation rate (µmol C m–2 leaf s–1). This ratio was 0.40–0.45 under drought, decreasing to 0.27–0.35 under re-irrigation (across inoculation treatments).
evidence: The claim is based on calculated ratios from experimental data.

claim: In irrigated saplings, the ratio between exudation rate and net assimilation rate increased from 0.12 to 0.17 without bacteria, to 0.34 and 0.58 in inoculated saplings.
source: In irrigated saplings, ratios increased from 0.12 to 0.17 without bacteria, to 0.34 and 0.58 in inoculated saplings (in later and earlier phases of the experiment, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on calculated ratios from experimental data.

claim: Roots of drought-exposed trees displayed substantial changes in exudate composition compared to irrigated trees, and more so when inoculated with rhizosphere bacteria.
source: Roots of drought-exposed trees displayed substantial changes in exudate composition compared to irrigated trees, and more so when inoculated with rhizosphere bacteria (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) showed that root exudates blends from drought trees that were inoculated and those from drought trees that were not inoculated partitioned into distinct clusters, with partial overlap.
source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) showed that root exudates blends (samples) from drought trees that were inoculated and those from drought trees that were not inoculated partitioned into distinct clusters, with partial overlap (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Metabolomics data identified 149 masses (52.6% of the total mass entities) that were significantly different from either Cupressus root tissues or a root-free control solution incubated in the soil, and were hence regarded as Cupressus exudates.
source: Metabolomics data identified 149 masses (52.6% of the total mass entities) that were significantly different from either Cupressus root tissues or a root-free control solution incubated in the soil, and were hence regarded as Cupressus exudates (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics analysis.

claim: About 30 of the identified metabolites were 2- to 10-fold more abundant in the exudates blends when compared to the controls.
source: About 30 of these metabolites were 2- to 10-fold more abundant in the exudates blends when compared to the controls, and the rest were 15- to 25-fold more abundant (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: 44 metabolites were significantly different between irrigated and drought trees (p<0.05).
source: Of the latter number, 44 metabolites were significantly different between irrigated and drought trees (p<0.05; Figure 3—source data 1), and 17 metabolites were significantly different between irrigated and re-irrigated trees (p<0.05) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: 17 metabolites were significantly different between irrigated and re-irrigated trees (p<0.05).
source: Of the latter number, 44 metabolites were significantly different between irrigated and drought trees (p<0.05; Figure 3—source data 1), and 17 metabolites were significantly different between irrigated and re-irrigated trees (p<0.05) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: 13 metabolites were significantly enriched or depleted following bacterial inoculation under drought.
source: In addition, 13 metabolites were significantly enriched or depleted following bacterial inoculation under drought and one metabolite changed following bacterial inoculation after re-irrigation (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: One metabolite changed following bacterial inoculation after re-irrigation.
source: In addition, 13 metabolites were significantly enriched or depleted following bacterial inoculation under drought and one metabolite changed following bacterial inoculation after re-irrigation (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: In two metabolites, the interaction irrigation:bacteria was significant under drought, but not under re-irrigation.

claim: Four lines of evidence support a mutual interaction between trees and bacteria: bacteria were physically attached to root surfaces; bacteria were always ~10-fold more abundant in the rhizosphere than the bulk soil; root exudation increased following inoculation, and was higher during drought than following it; and many metabolites were enriched following inoculation in drought trees.
source: Four lines of evidence in our study support a mutual interaction between trees and bacteria: (1) bacteria were physically attached to root surfaces; (2) bacteria were always ~10-fold more abundant in the rhizosphere than the bulk soil; (3) root exudation increased following inoculation, and was higher during drought than following it (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 7—source data 1); and (4) many metabolites were enriched following inoculation in drought trees.

claim: It is likely that both processes (exudates attracting bacteria and bacteria inducing root exudation) occurred simultaneously.
